name: Serbian Orthodox Church — Downtown Pest
description: The Church of Saint George on Szerb utca is the Serbian Orthodox parish church of central Pest and, according to Wikipedia, the only Serbian Orthodox church in the capital today. Its Baroque building dates from 1733, its tower from 1752, and its garden wall holds old Serbian gravestones.

children.text: The Serbian Orthodox Church of Saint George stands at Szerb utca 4, less than a hundred metres from Váci utca in the inner city. Its full Hungarian name is Szent György nagyvértanú szerb ortodox templom, and it belongs to the Eparchy of Buda of the Serbian Orthodox Church. English Wikipedia describes it as the only Serbian Orthodox church in the Hungarian capital today, and it is a protected monument. The street takes its name from the community: Szerb utca means Serbian Street.

Serbian worship in Pest is older than the present building. A Serbian place of worship stood here during the Ottoman period, and some sources suggest a church on the site even before 1526. After Habsburg forces took the town, that church was destroyed in 1686. The authorities permitted a new one in 1695, which Patriarch Arsenije III Čarnojević renovated in 1698. The Baroque church seen today was built in 1733 to plans by András Mayerhoffer, an architect from Salzburg, and the bell tower followed in 1752. Archaeological research in 1959 confirmed that it stands on the site of an older church.

Inside, the church follows the traditional layout of an Orthodox church, and Hungarian Wikipedia notes a wooden railing between the women's area and the men's area, which sits one step lower. The iconostasis seen today dates from 1850. The original, by Stefan Tenecki, was damaged in the flood of 1838 and was replaced by a Neo-Renaissance iconostasis by a Greek artist.

The surroundings are part of the character of the place. A Baroque garden is enclosed by a stone wall, and the gravestones of Serbs who were buried in Pest are built into it. A Copf-style gate on Szerb utca dates from 1776, and at the corner of Szerb utca and Veres Pálné utca a ceramic image of Saint George slaying the dragon sits in a niche in the wall.

The church also records how small the community's footprint became. The larger Church of Saint Demetrius, damaged in the Second World War, was demolished in 1949, which left this church as the city's only Serbian place of worship. It is still in active use: in 2021 the parish celebrated its patron saint with a hierarchal liturgy led by Bishop Lukijan of Buda, a procession around the church along Szerb utca and a programme in the courtyard.
Good to know
This is a working Serbian Orthodox church. Check access and service times with the parish before visiting, and do not assume the interior or garden is open to visitors.
It is under a hundred metres from Váci utca, so it fits easily into a walk through the inner city.
From the street, look for the ceramic image of Saint George at the corner of Szerb utca and Veres Pálné utca and for the tower added in 1752.

historyIntro: The Serbian Church of Saint George in central Pest was built in 1733 on the site of an older Serbian place of worship. It is the surviving centre of a Serbian community that settled in Pest after the Ottoman period.

historySections.heading: Serbs in Pest under Ottoman and Habsburg rule

children.text: English Wikipedia records that a Serbian place of worship stood on the site during Ottoman rule, and that some sources suggest a church existed even before the Battle of Mohács in 1526. A source from 1655 records a separate cemetery beside the Kecskemét Gate, and between 1660 and 1664 the Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi noted that the Serbs of Pest had their own church. After Habsburg forces captured the town, that church was destroyed in 1686. A new church was permitted in 1695, and Patriarch Arsenije III Čarnojević renovated it in 1698. Hungarian Wikipedia says the new church of 1695 to 1698 stood on the foundations of a medieval church.

A project for a new Baroque church was prepared in 1731, and Hungarian Wikipedia says the earlier church was demolished that year. The present church was built in 1733 to plans by András Mayerhoffer, an architect from Salzburg. The Baroque bell tower was completed in 1752, when the main facade also reached its present form. The Copf-style gate on Szerb utca was made in 1776. The original iconostasis was by Stefan Tenecki; after the flood of 1838 damaged it, a Neo-Renaissance iconostasis by a Greek artist was installed in 1850.

historySections.heading: Change and survival in the twentieth century

children.text: In 1932 the street level was raised and a new wrought-iron gate was made, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. After the Second World War the community's more significant church, Saint Demetrius, was demolished in 1949 following war damage, which left the church on Szerb utca as the only Serbian place of worship in the city. In 1959 archaeological research confirmed that the present building stands on the site of an older church. The church is protected by the Hungarian National Office for Cultural Heritage and remains in use by the Eparchy of Buda.

name: Queen of Heavens Church — Újpest
description: The Queen of Heavens Church, or Egek Királynéja-templom, is the main Roman Catholic parish church of Újpest. Built between 1875 and 1881 to plans by József Kauser in a neo-Gothic style, it stands on Szent István tér, the main square of a town founded only in 1840.

children.text: The Queen of Heavens Church, in Hungarian Egek Királynéja-templom, stands at Szent István tér 13 on the main square of the former town of Újpest, today Budapest's 4th district. It is the district's main Roman Catholic parish church. Since 1993 the parish has belonged to the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest; before that it was part of the Diocese of Vác.

Újpest is a young town by Budapest standards. It was founded in 1840 on land given by Count István Károlyi, north of Pest. Its Catholics were first a filial of Dunakeszi and later attached to the parish of Fót, until Bishop Antal József Peitler of Vác made the congregation an independent parish in February 1870. A parish house and Catholic school were completed in 1873, and the parish was formally organised in 1875 with Vince Illek as its first pastor. He served until his death in 1905.

The church was built between 1875 and 1881 in the neo-Gothic style, to plans by the architect József Kauser, with Károly Bachmann as builder. Hungarian Wikipedia notes that two side aisles and a tower were added later to the original building. The tower is integral to the church and the aisles are joined to the main structure.

The bells carry some of the church's recorded history. There were originally five, and the middle bell, which weighed 310 kilograms, was lost in the Second World War; its place in the bell frame remains empty. Four bells hang in the tower today. The largest, named for King Saint Stephen, weighs 1,010 kilograms and was cast in 1924 by Ferenc Walser. The other three were cast in 1888 by Walser as well.

The square around the church tells the story of the town. It was called Templom tér, the Church Square, until it was named Szent István tér in 1928, and it became Újpest's main square after the town hall opened in 1900. A Reformed church built in 1878 stands on one side, and the town hall and the Újpest market are also on the square. Újpest became part of Budapest in 1950.
Good to know
This is an active parish church. Check access and service times with the parish rather than assuming the interior is open to visitors.
Szent István tér also holds the Reformed church of 1878, the town hall by Henrik Bőhm and Ármin Hegedűs, and the Újpest market, so the square is worth a short walk in itself.
Újpest lies outside the central districts, so plan the journey with the public transport journey planner before you set out.

historyIntro: The Queen of Heavens Church was built between 1875 and 1881 for a town that had been founded only in 1840. Its history follows Újpest's growth from a filial congregation to a main parish church.

historySections.heading: A new town and its parish

children.text: Újpest was founded in 1840 on land given by Count István Károlyi, north of Pest. Until 1845 its Catholics were a filial of Dunakeszi, and then they were attached to the parish of Fót. In February 1870 Bishop Antal József Peitler of Vác made the Újpest congregation an independent parish. A parish house and a Catholic school were completed in 1873, and the parish was formally organised in 1875, with Vince Illek as its first pastor. He held the post until his death in 1905.

The church was built between 1875 and 1881, in the neo-Gothic style, to plans by József Kauser, with Károly Bachmann as builder. Two side aisles and a tower were added later to the original building. The tower is integral to the church and the aisles are joined to the main structure. Ferenc Walser cast the bells, three in 1888 and the largest, dedicated to King Saint Stephen, in 1924. A fifth, middle bell was lost in the Second World War.

The square in front of the church was called Templom tér, the Church Square, until it was named Szent István tér in 1928. It became the main square of Újpest after the town hall opened in 1900, and a Reformed church, built in 1878, stands on the same square. Újpest became part of Budapest in 1950, and in 1993 the parish passed from the Diocese of Vác to the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest.

name: Holy Family Church — Terézváros
description: The neo-Gothic Holy Family Church at Szondi utca 67 was built in 1930 and 1931 for a fast-growing Terézváros. Heavily damaged on New Year's Day 1945, it was rebuilt and reconsecrated in 1948, and its high altar was later clad in marble paid for by the composer Zoltán Kodály.

children.text: The Holy Family Church, Szent Család-templom in Hungarian, stands at Szondi utca 67 in Terézváros, Budapest's 6th district. It is a Roman Catholic parish church in the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest. Unlike the older churches of central Pest, it is a twentieth-century building: Hungarian Wikipedia explains that Budapest's population grew sharply between the two world wars, which created the need for a new church here.

The architect was Gáspár Fábián. The foundation stone was laid on 28 September 1930 and the church was consecrated on 15 November 1931 by the auxiliary bishop István Breyer. In 1933 the parish became a vicarage, and its first vicar, Ferenc Sármány, was also the church's builder. Hungarian Wikipedia calls the style neo-Gothic. The Budapest library's description is more detailed: an eclectic design based on medieval church architecture, with Romanesque-style elements on the facade and English Gothic details, such as a large Tudor-arched window between the towers.

On 1 January 1945 the church was severely damaged. Sources differ on the cause, one speaking of a bomb and another of a chained explosive, but they agree that the furnishings were lost, including the altars, pulpit and confessionals, and that the organ was partly destroyed. Two things survived: the crucifix beside the pulpit and a statue of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux. Reconstruction began in September 1947, and Bishop Zoltán Meszlényi reconsecrated the church on 18 May 1948.

Later additions give the interior its present character. In 1955 the composer Zoltán Kodály, who visited the church often, paid for the marble cladding of the high altar and the pulpit. Péter Barba painted a secco in the sanctuary in 1961, and a statue of the Rosa Mystica was installed in 1985. A columbarium for urns was built in the basement and courtyard in 1996, the building was renovated in 2000, two new bells were consecrated in 2002, Zsolt Boromisza painted two new seccos in 2003, and the organ was rebuilt in 2006.
Good to know
This is a working parish church. Check access and service times with the parish before visiting.
The columbarium in the basement and courtyard is part of the site, so ask the parish which areas are open to visitors.
From the street, look for the large Tudor-arched window between the two towers, which the library description picks out as an English Gothic detail.

historyIntro: The Holy Family Church was built in 1930 and 1931, destroyed in large part on New Year's Day 1945 and rebuilt by 1948. Its history is the story of a district church that was built, lost its furnishings and was gradually refitted.

historySections.heading: A church for the interwar city

children.text: Hungarian Wikipedia explains that Budapest's population grew significantly between the two world wars, which created the need for a new church at Szondi utca 67. The architect was Gáspár Fábián. The foundation stone was laid on 28 September 1930, and the church was consecrated on 15 November 1931 by the auxiliary bishop István Breyer. In 1933 the parish became a vicarage, and its first vicar, Ferenc Sármány, was also the builder of the church.

On 1 January 1945, during the Second World War, the church was struck and severely damaged. Hungarian Wikipedia speaks of a bomb, and the Budapest library's description of a chained explosive. The altars, pulpit, confessionals and lighting were destroyed, and the organ was partly destroyed. Only the crucifix beside the pulpit and a statue of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux survived. Reconstruction began in September 1947, and on 18 May 1948 Bishop Zoltán Meszlényi reconsecrated the church.

In 1955 Zoltán Kodály, who visited the church often, paid for the marble cladding of the high altar and the pulpit. Péter Barba painted a secco in the sanctuary in 1961, and insulation work was carried out in the 1970s. A statue of the Rosa Mystica was installed in 1985, and a columbarium was built in the basement and courtyard in 1996. The church was renovated in 2000, two new bells were consecrated in 2002, Zsolt Boromisza painted two new seccos in 2003 and the organ was restored in 2006.
